1:
That the prayer follows the sermon is noticed by all, and each draws a different lesson. Chrysostom sees a pattern for the tempted: having said the world would bring tribulation, Christ "betaketh Himself to prayer, teaching us in our temptations to leave all things, and flee to God"; the disciples "most of all needed to be established." Calvin makes it a rule for teachers: "doctrine has no power, if efficacy be not imparted to it from above", so preachers must mingle prayer with their sowing. Henry counts four things it was at once: a prayer after a sermon ("those we preach to we must pray for"), after sacrament, a family prayer, a parting prayer.

The lifted eyes are read as instruction, not posture. Chrysostom says Christ looked up "to teach us intentness in our prayers: that we should stand with uplifted eyes, not of the body only, but of the mind", and notes that "the Evangelist doth not even call the action prayer", but a discoursing with the Father. Augustine puts it more sharply: Christ "could have prayed in silence had He pleased; but He remembered that He had not only to pray, but to teach", the prayer being "for His disciples' edification, yes and for ours who read the same." Calvin denies that heaven contains God: the attitude means only that Christ "was rather in heaven than in earth, so that, leaving men behind him, he conversed familiarly with God."

Where the words were spoken divides them. Barnes and Clarke place the party on the road: the prayer was offered "in the stillness of the night, in the open air", Clarke picturing our Lord "still moving on towards Gethsemane, not having yet passed the brook Cedron". Ellicott keeps them indoors, the prayer uttered "as they were preparing to leave the chamber after supper", since "to heaven" need not "imply that he looked up to the sky, and must, therefore, have been in the open air" — "the upward look is naturally expressive of feeling, and irrespective of place."

"The hour is come" draws the chapter's one flat refusal. Augustine reads it as proof "that all time, and every thing that He did or suffered to be done, was at His disposing" — yet by God's ordering, "not that we must suppose that this hour came by any fatal necessity" — then turns on the astrologers: "away with the notion, that the stars could doom to death the Creator of the stars." Hilary presses the noun: not the day nor the time but the hour, and "an hour contains a portion of a day". Bede fixes the seam: the earlier discourse was spoken sitting, this hymn standing.

The high-priestly reading belongs to Clarke and Ellicott. Clarke lays it over the Day of Atonement: the high priest washed and put on clean linen, which Christ imitates in laying aside his garments; then prayed for himself, then for the sons of Aaron, then for the people — the prayer's three movements exactly. Ellicott calls it the High Priest's Prayer and warns that "he is in the Holy of Holies, and must approach it with eyes and heart uplifted".

Barnes calls it "the longest prayer recorded in the New Testament" and "perhaps the most sublime composition to be found anywhere", glossing the petition: "give to the world demonstration that I am thy Son". Robertson notes that "glorify thy Son" is "the only personal petition in this prayer", and rejects the critical alternative outright: "it is inconceivable that this is the free composition of a disciple put into the mouth of Jesus." Wesley hears the bare address as decisive — "this simplicity of appellation highly became the only-begotten Son of God" — and notes that "when he speaks to the Father he does not style himself the Son of man." Gill refers the opening words back to the three chapters of comfort just ended.
2:
Verse 2 sets the sharpest doctrinal division in the chapter, and it runs along confessional lines. Clarke reads the grant as universal in intent: "all flesh, i.e. all the human race, was given unto him, that by one sacrifice of himself, he might reconcile them all to God"; since all "were delivered into his power", "the design of God is that all should have eternal life". Wesley agrees flatly: the verse is "a clear proof that Christ designed his sacrifice should avail for all: yea, that all flesh, every man, should partake of everlasting life."

Calvin reads the same two clauses as deliberately unequal. Authority is universal, the gift is not: "Christ does not say that he has been made Governor over the whole world, in order to bestow on all without any distinction; but he limits this grace to those who" were given. To the objection that the Father has subjected the reprobate to him as well, he answers that "it is only the elect who belong to his peculiar flock, which he has undertaken to guard as a Shepherd" — the kingdom extends to all, the shepherding does not. Barnes, without Calvin's vocabulary, marks the same seam: the Saviour "makes an important distinction between 'all flesh' and those who were 'given him'", the first a dominion that restrains, the second a purpose that saves. Gill takes the power as delegated, not native: "not that original power over all things he has as God... but a derived and delegated power, which he has as Mediator."

Ellicott and Robertson keep to the grammar and confirm the asymmetry from it. Ellicott notes "all flesh" renders a Hebrew idiom signifying "humanity as such, considered in its weakness and imperfection"; more tellingly, the "all" given is "a neuter singular, and signifies collectively the whole body of humanity given to Christ", while the pronoun for those receiving is "masculine and plural, and signifies the individual reception". Robertson calls the claim to authority over all flesh "stupendous... impossible for a mere man to make", made twice elsewhere and repeated after the resurrection.

On eternal life the company converges. Barnes insists the knowing is not speculative but includes "all the impressions on the mind and life which a just view of God and of the Saviour is fitted to produce", and guards the exclusive clause: "the only God, in opposition to all false gods... in opposition to idols, not to Jesus himself." Wesley says the same in miniature: the phrase excludes "the false gods of the heathens", not the Son and Spirit, and the knowledge is "both the way to, and the essence of, everlasting happiness". Calvin makes the knowledge itself the life, "not every kind of knowledge... but that knowledge which forms us anew into the image of God", which "is the same with faith". Ellicott renders it "recognise Thee as the only true God", and reads the verses as a sequence: the work is to give life, this is what the giving consists in, the next says it is done.

Clarke gives four reasons the salvation is called life — a forfeited life redeemed, souls dead in trespasses quickened, the unsaved merely existing since "no good purpose of life being answered by them", and a reach beyond time implying the soul's immortality and the body's resurrection. Robertson flags the real difficulty, that "Jesus Christ" in the Lord's own prayer is odd, and offers the way out that Christ is a predicate accusative — "Jesus as the Christ" — else the words look like the evangelist's parenthesis. Origen, worrying the same knot from the other end, presses John's careful use of the article, which he says is added when the name of God "refers to the uncreated cause of all things" and omitted when the Logos is named God — a distinction offered to those "afraid that they may be proclaiming two Gods".
4:
"I have finished the work" is spoken before the cross, and every commentator has to say how. Barnes reads the perfect as reaching forward: "when he says 'I have finished,' he probably means to include also his death" — and turns it into a lesson: "how happy would it be if men would imitate his example, and not leave their great work of life to be done on a dying bed!" Calvin says the same more exactly: "the sacrifice of death, by which he was to take away the iniquities of us all", still remained, "yet, as the hour of his death was already at hand, he speaks as if he had already endured it." Clarke has Christ considering himself "as already sacrificed for the sin of the world". Wesley compresses the whole into a clause: thus have I glorified thee, "laying the foundation of thy kingdom on earth."

Robertson turns the same verb against a modern reading: "now as he faces death he has no sense of failure as some modern critics say, but rather fulness of attainment" — he "does not die as a disappointed man, but as the successful messenger". Ellicott keeps the two clauses tied — the first "is explained by the latter", since "God was glorified in the completion of the Messianic work of Christ", the work including "the whole life as manifesting God to man". Gill spreads the glorifying across ministry, miracles and conduct, the miracles themselves referred by Christ to the Father.

Verse 5 draws the chapter's strongest christological statements, unusually concordant. Barnes calls it the most distinct declaration of pre-existence there could be: "before the creation of the world; before there was any world... equivalent to saying that he existed from eternity" — the glory being that "proper to the Son of God", laid aside when he "emptied himself". Ellicott allows the words one sense only: Christ "claimed for Himself the possession of the divine glory in His pre-existent state", "in personality distinct from, but in essence one with God"; and since this is said by Christ himself in prayer, no reading of these verses "denies that our Lord Jesus Christ claimed for Himself that He was divine, and co-eternal with the Father."

Robertson insists the pre-existence is "not just ideal... but actual and conscious existence at the Father's side", and notes that even a hostile critic conceded the words reflect the certainty with which Jesus spoke. Wesley makes the point with one verb: "he does not say received — he always had it, till he emptied himself of it in the days of his flesh." Clarke paraphrases: let "the glory of my eternal divinity surround and penetrate my humanity, in its resurrection, ascension, and in the place which it is to occupy at thy right hand."

Calvin is careful about what is requested. Christ "desires nothing that does not strictly belong to him, but only that he may appear in the flesh, such as he was before the creation of the world" — the Divine majesty "which he had always possessed" now "illustriously displayed in the person of the Mediator, and in the human flesh with which he was clothed". From this he infers that Christ "is not a God who has been newly contrived, or who has existed only for a time", and that "a manifest distinction between the person of Christ and the person of the Father is here expressed". Cyril of Jerusalem uses the verse for a distinction the others do not raise: God is Father of men "in an improper sense", by care rather than begetting, but "of Christ alone He is the Father by nature, not by adoption... of men in time, but of Christ before all time." Gill notes the request is not for the divine perfections, which dwelt in him already, but for the glorious presence at the right hand.
6:
Chrysostom takes the verse as explaining the last: having said "I have finished Thy work", Christ "next explaineth it in detail, telling what sort of work" — announcing the Father, which is why the Son is called the messenger of great counsel. He anticipates the objection that the name was known already: "though it was known, yet it was so only to Jews, and not to all of these: but now He speaketh concerning the Gentiles." And it went further than monotheism: "it is not the same thing to learn that He is Creator, and that He hath a Son".

Augustine raises a difficulty nobody else notices, and leaves it open. If the words cover only the eleven at supper, they cannot be the glorifying spoken of above: "for what great glory... was it to become known to twelve, or rather eleven mortal creatures?" If they cover all who would ever believe, this is indeed the Son glorifying the Father, "the past being put for the future". He leans wider, then concedes that "what follows shows that He is speaking here of those who were already His disciples."

What "out of the world" means divides them. Clarke restricts it nationally — "from among the Jewish people; for in this sense is the word kosmos to be understood in our Lord's last discourses" — the men being the apostles. Ellicott makes the separation moral, not ethnic: the disciples are "a body separated from the world" and given by the Father. Calvin makes it elective and confronts the tension: Christ's preaching "was common to all", so why say he manifested the name only to a few? "Because the elect alone profit by the grace of the Spirit, who teaches inwardly." Robertson keeps the plain historical sense: "Jesus regards the apostles as the Father's gift to him", recalling the night of prayer before he chose them.

"Thine they were" gets three incompatible glosses. Barnes takes creation and providence: "all men are God's by creation and by preservation." Wesley takes it "by creation, and by descent from Abraham". Ellicott takes it of prior moral preparation: "they were morally prepared by the earlier manifestation of God for the fuller manifestation in Christ", so that "when Christ was revealed to them, they recognised Him of whom Moses and the prophets did speak." Clarke reads election, "objects of thy choice".

On the disciples' knowledge, Robertson and Ellicott both catch the tense and soften the claim. Ellicott renders "now they do know" — "they have come to know, and do know" — the fruit of a training still future in its fulness "but regarded as in the immediate present". Robertson agrees: "not as fully as they felt, and yet in a real sense"; Christ "claims loyalty and fidelity in these men with the one exception of Judas. He does not claim perfection for them." Ellicott refuses to narrow it — "we ought to assign no limit to the extent of these words" — what they came to know being that "the whole life of Christ... was a manifestation of the Father."

Calvin finds here the chief part of faith, which "does not rest satisfied with beholding the flesh, but perceives his Divine power"; for "if we do not perceive God in Christ, we must remain continually in a state of hesitation." On words given and received, Ellicott balances the halves — "I, on My part, have given unto them", "they on their part received them" — since "others had been taught, and did not receive. The teaching was the same; the varying effect was in the heart of the hearer." Robertson marks the refrain "thou didst send me" recurring five times. Clarke stresses the deposit's purity: "neither Jewish fables nor fictions of men have been mingled with it." Gill lists the titles the doctrine bears in Scripture; Wesley reduces receiving to "by faith."
9:
"I pray not for the world" is the prayer's hardest clause, and the readings fan out widely. Ellicott and Robertson narrow it temporally. Ellicott insists on the strict present — "I am praying for them: I am not praying for the world" — referring "to the prayer which He is at this moment uttering, and not to His general practice". Robertson says the same: "now at this point in the prayer Christ means" — God loves the whole world, and Christ "died for sinners and prayed for sinners." Wesley argues from parity: this no more proves Christ did not pray for the world "than his praying for the apostles alone... proves that he did not pray for them which shall believe through their word."

Clarke narrows it historically. Christ is "wholly employed for my disciples", as the high priest's second petition on the day of expiation was for the sons of Aaron; the words may also cover the rebellious Jews. Barnes narrows it morally — the world means "wicked, perverse, rebellious men" — so the passage "settles nothing about the question whether Christ prayed for sinners."

Augustine reads a definition of the world, not a limit on the prayer. Christ means "those who live according to the lust of the world, and stand not in the gracious lot of such as were to be chosen by Him out of the world"; "by the very fact of their having already been given Him by the Father, they have ceased to belong to that world." Chrysostom finds love rather than limit: Christ "not only gives them what He has of His own, but entreats another for them, as a still further proof of His love".

Calvin alone feels the objection's full weight. No better rule of prayer exists than to follow Christ, yet "we are commanded to pray for all", and Christ himself prayed indiscriminately from the cross. His reply: "the prayers which we offer for all are still limited to the elect of God" — we pray for this man and that, and so include the race, not knowing who is who. Henry works the distinction through a farming image: take the world for "a heap of unwinnowed corn in the floor, and God loves it, Christ prays for it, and dies for it, for a blessing is in it"; but the Lord "eyes particularly those that were given him out of the world, extracts them", and the world then means the remaining heap.

Verse 10 is read as a claim no creature could make. Wesley calls them "very high and strong expressions, too grand for any mere creature to use", implying that all things, "inclusive of the Divine nature, perfections, and operations, are the common property of the Father and the Son." Robertson catches that the Greek verb is singular, "emphasizing the unity of the whole". Ellicott corrects the English: the pronouns are not masculine, so the words are "all-inclusive, and assert absolute community in all things between the Father and the Son", and he treats the clause as parenthesis. Gill takes the opposite line — "Christ is speaking not of things but of persons" — the mutual interest arising "from an union in nature, an agreement in covenant, and a conjunction in operation".

Calvin draws out the assurance: Christ pleads for none but those the Father owns, "for I have nothing separated from thee, and therefore I shall not meet with a refusal"; and "we shall not be satisfied with having Christ, if we do not know that we possess God in him." Robertson finds comfort in the perfect tense — "I stand glorified in the disciples, in spite of all their shortcomings and failings." Cyril of Jerusalem puts the clause to creedal use, citing it to show "no opposition in those who work", the Son reigning over a workmanship the Father could have made alone.
11:
The petition turns on a textual question, and the moderns agree against the received English. Clarke reports that a great weight of manuscripts reads a relative agreeing with name, giving "keep them through thy own name which thou hast given me", the name meaning "the doctrine or knowledge of the true God" — a reading of "the most ample evidence and indisputable authority". Ellicott calls the text "slightly doubtful" but adopts the same rendering; Robertson supplies the grammar. Barnes, on the older text, still resists "keep by thy power": it is literally "keep in thy name" — "keep in the knowledge of thyself... suffer them not to fall away from thee and to become apostates." Wesley keeps the instrumental sense: "thy power, mercy, wisdom".

Why the prayer is needed now is put best by Calvin: the disciples "will very soon be deprived of his bodily presence, under which they had reposed till now." So long as he dwelt with them "he cherished them, as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings"; the consolation is that the Son "becomes so much the more earnest about the salvation of his people, when he leaves them as to his bodily presence". Ellicott fixes the interval: the words look to the time "between His death and the day of Pentecost", "a time of darkness and danger". Robertson notes that "Holy Father" occurs nowhere else in the New Testament; Ellicott finds the epithet exactly fitted, standing "in opposition to the world" in which the disciples are left. Henry observes what the petitions are not: not "that they might be rich and great in the world... but that they might be kept from sin, and furnished for their duty, and brought safely to heaven" — "Christ's intercession is always pertinent."

On the oneness prayed for, Barnes says the comparison "refers not to a union of nature, but of feeling, plan, purpose. Any other union between Christians is impossible"; Wesley adds "by resemblance to us, though not equality", the disciples being "one body, separate from the world".

Ellicott distinguishes the two verbs of verse 12: kept points "to the preservation in the truth revealed to them", guarded "to the watchfulness by means of which this result was obtained" — feeding the flock, and guarding it "from the wild beasts around". Robertson takes the second literally: "Christ was the sentinel for them." Calvin faces the objection that Christ seems to hand over the office of keeping: "he speaks here of visible guardianship only which ended at the death of Christ", all of it belonging "to the person of the Mediator, who appeared, for a time, under the form of a servant". Gill guards it from the other side: the leaving is bodily, for "Christ is with his people whilst they are on earth, and they are with him when he is in heaven".

Judas produces the real quarrel. Wesley reads the exception as decisive against unconditional decree: "so one even of them whom God had given him is lost. So far was even that decree from being unchangeable!" — and glosses the title as one "that deservedly perishes". Barnes blocks the inference by narrowing the giving: the words are used "in the sense of giving as apostles", and "do not of necessity prove that they were true believers", Christ having already called one of the twelve a devil. Clarke presses the difficulty rather than dissolving it — Judas "was first given by God to Christ. But why was he lost?" — answering from an older father that he would not be saved, and might even after the betrayal "have returned to God and have found mercy". Robertson keeps to the words: the phrase is the very one used of antichrist, marking "final loss, not annihilation, but meeting one's destiny"; and it is unclear whether the appeal to Scripture is the evangelist's comment or Christ's own.
13:
Calvin explains why the prayer is spoken aloud, and the answer is pastoral. Christ was earnest "not that he was anxious about their future condition, but rather to provide a remedy for their anxiety"; he prays in their hearing "not because he needed any words, but to remove from them all doubt". Ellicott adds the consequence for reading: they were to have "the support of knowing that He who had kept them while with them, had solemnly committed them to His Father's care" — "the prayer itself was a lesson."

The joy is defined three ways. Barnes takes it prospectively, of the joy resulting "from his resurrection, ascension, and intercession"; Ellicott takes it of Christ's own, "that which supported Him in all the sorrow and loneliness of His work on earth"; Robertson reads the perfect participle: "that they may keep on having Christ's joy... realized in themselves".

On the world's hatred Chrysostom turns to counsel: "when having become virtuous we are persecuted by the wicked... let us not be distracted or angry. For this is the natural course of things, and everywhere virtue is wont to engender hatred from wicked men." The hatred is a mark of virtue, against which he sets the woe on those of whom all men speak well.

Augustine explains the tense: the disciples "had not yet experienced these sufferings", but Christ speaks "in His usual way, foretelling the future in words of the past tense". Their not being of the world "was conferred on them by regeneration; for by generation they were of the world" — with one asymmetry: Christ "was never of the world", receiving even the form of a servant from the Spirit by whom they were born again. Ellicott makes the connection causal: "the world's hatred followed necessarily from the fact that Christ had given them God's word." Clarke localises the hostility to "the Jewish rulers" and closes on human nature: "men despise that which they should esteem, and endeavor to destroy that without which they must be destroyed themselves!" Gill finds the reason in the word, which "magnifies the grace of God, and destroys boasting".

Robertson turns the double preposition into indictment. The disciples are in the world and sent into it, "but they must not be like the world nor get their spirit, standards, and message out of the world, else they can do the world no good" — verses which "go far towards explaining the failure of Christians in winning the world."

Why the disciples are left in danger rather than removed is answered in one voice and several accents. Barnes: God could remove his people at once to heaven, "but it is better for them to remain, and show the power of religion in supporting the soul in the midst of trial". Clarke adds that Christ does not wish his apostles secluded "by going to the desert, or to the cloisters". Ellicott gives the series: "the Christian ideal is not freedom from work, but strength to do it; not freedom from temptation, but power to overcome it; not freedom from suffering, but joy in an abiding sense of the Father's love." Calvin rules out the wish: safety does not mean believers are "free from every annoyance, and live in luxury and at their ease", but that "in the midst of dangers, they continue to be safe"; so "we must not desire exemption from evils". Gill adds that work remained, and their living longer "would make most for his glory".

"The evil" is left open. Robertson notes it "can mean the evil man, Satan, or the evil deed", the ambiguity of the Lord's Prayer; Clarke and Wesley take it personally, of "the evil one, who reigns therein". Calvin reads the repetition of verse 16 as arguing that the hatred "does not arise from any fault of theirs, but because the world hates God and Christ."
17:
What "sanctify" asks for is the question, and answers range from separation to renewal. Ellicott is most decided: "the idea at the root of the word rendered 'sanctify' is not holiness, but separation. It is opposed not to what is impure, but to what is common" — the Old Testament word for consecrating persons and things to God, which is why Christ can use it of himself. Robertson agrees, "to consecrate or set apart persons or things to God", done "in the sphere of truth... God's message to us". Barnes and Clarke take both senses at once. Clarke distinguishes them — to separate "from earth and common use", and "to make holy or pure" — applying each to the ministry: they are to be "fully consecrated to the work", and "patterns of all holiness". Barnes describes progressive sanctification as "becoming more like God and less attached to the world", adds the official sense, and connects them: "ministers will be really devoted to God just in proportion as they are personally pure."

Calvin and Henry take renewal rather than office. Calvin glosses it as God renewing us by his Spirit, consecrating the disciples "entirely to himself" and defending them "as his sacred inheritance". Henry unfolds three requests: that God confirm the work — "strengthen their faith, inflame their good affections, rivet their good resolutions" — that he carry it on, and "crown it with the perfection of holiness". Gill hears both; Wesley holds both in a line: "consecrate them by the anointing of thy Spirit to their office, and perfect them in holiness."

On the means, Calvin turns polemical in both directions. There are "fanatics who indulge in much useless prattle" about sanctification while neglecting the word by which God consecrates us, and others who "chatter quite as foolishly" about the word while disregarding Christ; against both, the instrument is the Gospel doctrine the apostles had heard and were to preach. Ellicott makes the point spatially: truth "was the sphere in which their sanctification was to take place", a region into which they had already passed.

Verse 18 is read as identity of calling. Calvin puts it as Christ's argument: "the calling of Christ and of the apostles is the same calling" — "I now appoint them to an office, which I have hitherto held by thy command; and, therefore, it is necessary that they should be furnished with the power of thy Spirit." Clarke says the apostles "had the same commission which Christ had, considered as man"; Ellicott notes the mission is already contained in the word apostle.

"I sanctify myself" is the tightest problem, since Christ had no impurity to remove; the solution is unanimous. Barnes: "the word sanctify does not refer here to personal sanctification, for he had no sin, but to setting himself apart entirely to the work of redemption." Wesley makes it a sacrifice: "I devote myself as a victim, to be sacrificed"; Clarke the same, with the priestly figure: "I consecrate and devote myself to death", entering "into the holiest of all by his own blood". Ellicott adds that Christ thus enters, "as both Priest and Sacrifice", the heavenly Holy of Holies.

Calvin traces the transfer: "because he consecrated himself to the Father... his holiness might come to us; for as the blessing on the first-fruits is spread over the whole harvest, so the Spirit of God cleanses us by the holiness of Christ" — and not "by imputation only", since he "presented us to his Father in his own person, that we may be renewed by his Spirit". Robertson enters the caution: "the act of Christ helps us, but by no means takes the place of personal consecration on the part of the believer", turning it on those who use "the livery of heaven to serve the devil in".
20:
The widening of the prayer is felt as personal by nearly all. Augustine takes "all" to mean "not only those who were then alive, but those who were to be born; not those only who heard the Apostles themselves, but us who were born long after their death." He then notices what nobody else does: on a strict reading some are left out, those who "believed already" without hearing the apostles' word — was Nathanael of that number, or Joseph of Arimathea? Chrysostom finds a comfort for the eleven, "that they were to be the cause of the salvation of others".

Barnes turns it to consolation: "it is a matter of unspeakable joy that each Christian, however humble or unknown to men, can reflect that he was remembered in prayer by him whom God heareth always." Calvin makes it assurance, with a sea image: "this prayer of Christ is a safe harbour, and whoever retreats into it is safe from all danger of shipwreck; for it is as if Christ had solemnly sworn that he will devote his care and diligence to our salvation." The order is deliberate: Christ "began with his apostles, that their salvation... might make us more certain of our own". Henry states the limiting principle: "those, and those only, are interested in the mediation of Christ, that do, or shall, believe in him."

Ellicott records that the best manuscripts read a present, "them also which believe", the Church's future being "so immediately in our Lord's thoughts that it is spoken of as actually present". Robertson makes the agency the point, with an edge: preaching is "an agency sadly limited by the lives of those who speak in Christ's name."

What kind of unity is prayed for divides them. Ellicott presses the grammar hardest. The word "art" is not in the text; the second "one" "is of doubtful authority, and has the appearance of a gloss", so the probable reading runs "that they all may be one; as Thou, Father, in Me, and I in Thee, that they also may be in Us" — the Church's union being "of the same essential nature as that between the Father and the Son", resulting "from the union of individual members with the Father through the Son". Augustine fixes the same limit from the other side: Christ "did not say that we all may be one, but, that they all may be one" — the comparison holds of manner, not measure. Wesley makes it a rule of reading: the words are "to be understood in a way of similitude, and not of sameness or equality".

Robertson draws the consequence: "the only possible way to have unity among believers is for all of them to find unity first with God in Christ"; "strife, wrangling, division are a stumblingblock to the outside world." Clarke observes that the prayer "was literally answered to the first believers, who were all of one heart and of one soul", then asks: "why is it that believers are not in the same spirit now? Because they neither attend to the example nor to the truth of Christ." He restricts the unity to spirit and privilege, not outward form. Gill distributes it likewise, looking to "the latter day, when saints shall see eye to eye".

Calvin sets it in a larger frame: "the ruin of the human race is, that, having been alienated from God, it is also broken and scattered in itself", so restoration "consists in its being properly united in one body". Henry gives the sequence its logic: purity first, "for the wisdom from above is first pure, then peaceable". Wesley closes by summarising the prayer — receive me into thy glory, let my apostles share it, and all other believers, "and let all the world believe" — and, against his own reading of verse 9: "here Christ prays for the world."
22:
"The glory which thou gavest me I have given them" is defined five ways. Gill works by elimination — not the deity's glory; not the mediatorial glory, which "is not given to the saints"; not the power of miracles, since "all that are his have not had it, and some have had it who are none of his" — and settles on the Gospel. Clarke also rejects the miraculous reading, since Christ prays here for all who would believe, and offers "the glorious privilege of becoming sons of God; that, being all adopted children of the same Father, they may abide in peace, love, and unity" — or else that the glory is heaven's.

Ellicott takes that alternative: "the fulness of the glory which awaits Him at His Father's right hand is thought of as already given to Him", the believers united to him being "sharers in it". Barnes keeps it relational, "the honour which thou hast conferred on me by admitting me to union with thee, the same honour I have conferred on them". Robertson makes a distinction the others miss: this is "the glory of the Incarnate Word", not the Eternal Word's glory which verse 24 will name.

On the oneness Barnes is careful to say what it is not: not union "in nature, or in the mode of existence — for this was not the subject of discourse, and would be impossible — but in feeling, in principle, in purpose", the Father and Son having "always... sought the same object", the model "on which Christians should act." His gloss on perfect in one is mechanical: "a machine is perfect or complete when it has all its parts and is in good order", so the union would be complete "if there were no controversies, no envyings, no contentions". Christ, foreseeing how prone they were "to mistake love of sect or party for zeal for pure religion", pressed union on them when about to die.

Ellicott treats "I in them, and thou in me" as parenthesis, and states a rule of reading for the whole discourse: the words "were not uttered as separate words and phrases, but... were spoken as a whole, and should be read as a whole; and... the most unfathomable of them were spoken in prayer from the Son to the Father." He also corrects the rendering — better "perfected unto one", since "the unity is the result of their being made perfect" — confirmed by Robertson from the tense.

Calvin makes the glory a defaced likeness restored. Christ "had nothing that belonged peculiarly to himself, but rather was rich, in order to enrich those who believed in him"; our happiness "lies in having the image of God restored and formed anew in us, which was defaced by sin"; and the Father's likeness is engraved even on the human nature "which he has in common with us". The consequence is a test: "no one ought to be reckoned among the disciples of Christ, unless we perceive impressed on him, as with a seal, the likeness of Christ." The world, he adds, is "compelled to feel, whether it will or not", the love of God "when the Holy Spirit dwelling in them sends forth the rays of righteousness and holiness"; and the Father's love toward the Head "is extended to all the members, so that he loves none but in Christ."

Robertson grounds the world's knowing in conduct, the love "illustrated and proven by the way Christians love one another"; Clarke narrows the audience, "that the Jewish people first, and secondly the Gentiles, may acknowledge me as the true Messiah"; Wesley draws the inference the others leave implicit: "the glory of the only begotten shines in all the sons of God." Gill names the indwelling personal: Christ is in his people "as the head in the members, as the master of the house".
24:
Everything turns on "I will", and the readings run from demand to desire. Gill takes demand: the form is "not so much by way of entreaty, as demand", Christ insisting "on it as his right, upon the foot of his purchase, and those covenant transactions which passed between him and his Father". Barnes takes the opposite: the expression, "though it commonly denotes command, is here only expressive of desire... it was not the custom of the Saviour to use language of command when addressing God" — it is "a pressing and importunate wish". Calvin agrees, "it expresses not a command but a prayer". Ellicott and Robertson locate the force in identity of will rather than tone: for Ellicott it "expresses the consciousness that His will was that of the Father"; for Robertson it is "perfect identity of his will with that of the Father", though at Gethsemane Christ will distinguish the two. Henry marks it untransferable: "he speaks a language peculiar to himself, and such as does not become ordinary petitioners." Wesley says it in six words: he "prays, not as a servant, but a Son".

Augustine builds the verse into an argument for hope. The present "is not a life to be loved, but to be tolerated", and the hearer needs "the power of patient endurance amid all its tribulation" — so "listen, believe, hope, desire what He saith". He reasons from the unity of will that the petition cannot fail: "nor can that but be done, which the Almighty Son says that He wishes to the Almighty Father: for the Father and the Son have one will, which, if weakness prevent us from comprehending, piety must believe." He glosses "where I am" as "where He was shortly to be, i.e. heaven". Chrysostom sets it in sequence: after promising many converts and great glory, Christ "then speaks of the crowns in store for them".

Henry reads the order of petitions as a rule of prayer. Christ had asked preservation, sanctification and unity, "and now he prays that he would crown all his gifts with their glorification. In this method we must pray, first for grace, and then for glory; for in this method God gives."

What "behold my glory" promises is contested only in degree. Barnes says the word "implies more than simply seeing; it means also to participate, to enjoy"; Clarke the same, "that they may enjoy eternal felicity with me in thy kingdom". Calvin canvasses the alternatives — Christ's eternal presence, reception into the kingdom, partaking of what Christ has, knowing by faith "how great is his majesty" — and settles on "the perfect happiness of believers, as if he had said, that his desire will not be satisfied till they have been received into heaven." He then gives the finest image here: at present they saw the glory "just as a man shut up in the dark obtains, through small chinks, a feeble and glimmering light", where Christ now asks that they "enjoy the full brightness of heaven". Robertson keeps the present tense, "that they may keep on beholding", the joy endless.

The closing clause is taken by all as pre-existence. Barnes calls it "another of the numerous passages which prove that the Lord Jesus existed before the creation of the world. It is not possible to explain it on any other supposition." Robertson finds here "the same pre-incarnate consciousness of Christ" as in verse 5, while Ellicott distinguishes the two, the added words showing that the glory beheld is "the future glory of the divine-human nature of Christ". Cyril of Jerusalem presses the point creedally: the Son "began not His being when He was born in Bethlehem, but Before All Ages". From the prophet's "goings forth... from days of eternity" he concludes, "think not then of Him who is now come forth out of Bethlehem, but worship Him who was eternally begotten of the Father."
25:
Why the Father is addressed as righteous rather than holy is answered four ways. Ellicott ties it to the petition just made: that they behold the divine glory raises the difficulty "that sinful humanity cannot see God and live", so the appeal is to righteousness. Gill grounds it in the divine nature, righteousness being "a perfection of it", so Christ "might justly expect that all his petitions and claims... would be regarded". Wesley draws the sharpest inference: "the admission of believers to God through Christ, flows even from the justice of God." Robertson notes the parallel with the holiness invoked at verse 11.

Calvin turns the epithet into defiance. By calling him righteous, Christ "defies the world and its malice; as if he had said, 'However proudly the world may despise or reject God, still it takes nothing from him, and cannot hinder the honor of his righteousness from remaining unimpaired.'" Hence a rule of faith: it "ought to be founded on God, in such a manner that, though the world should oppose, it would never fail". Christ pleads "with peculiar warmth" for those whom the world's unbelief "did not prevent from acknowledging God".

Robertson catches a connective everyone else drops: translations "usually slur over" it "as untranslatable in English", but it may be "almost concessive like 'though'" — "though the world did not know thee, yet I knew thee, and these knew thee." Ellicott renders the tense strictly, "the world indeed knew Thee not"; Clarke lists what the disciples are credited with: receiving him as Messiah, the Father made known, and a purpose "to continue to influence them by the Spirit of truth".

The last verse divides on the future declaring. Barnes takes the interval after Easter, "after my resurrection, and by the influence of the Holy Spirit"; Clarke names both channels, the conversations "during the space of forty days" and the outpouring at Pentecost. Ellicott links it to the previous verse, the verb sharing its root with known: the teaching "had been a making known of the name, character, will of God", received "in part only". Robertson calls it "the perpetual mission of Christ through the Spirit". Calvin agrees the teaching was never bare speech — Christ "employed the secret revelation of the Spirit, and not the sound of his voice alone" — and, their faith being "very weak", the promise prepares them for "more abundant grace of the Holy Spirit".

On the closing petition Ellicott raises the claim as high as it goes: "it is more than that God may love the disciples, even as He loved the Son; it is that they may so know the nature of God that this love may be in them, dwelling in them as the principle of their life." Calvin puts it as union: "apart from Christ, we are hated by God, and he only begins to love us, when we are united to the body of his beloved Son." Wesley reads it reciprocally, "that they may love me with that love", the name declared being God's "new, best name of love". Gill notes that nothing of God "is to be known savingly, but in and through Christ".

Barnes and Clarke both close on the discourse as a whole. Barnes calls it "the most tender and sublime that was ever pronounced in our world", no composition being "so fitted to sustain the soul in trial or to support it in death", the prayer that ends it "the model for our prayers". Clarke sets it against the Sermon on the Mount: that one "shows men what they should do, so as to please God: this sermon shows them how they are to do the things prescribed in the other. In the former the reader sees a strict morality which he fears he shall never be able to perform: in this, all things are possible to him who believes."
